response.passage: Satellites are remarkable tools that orbit our planet to help us in daily life. Unlike airplanes that rely on air to generate lift, rockets use powerful engines to eject fuel, allowing them to travel through the vacuum of space where there is no air to push against. Once a satellite reaches its orbit, it does not need its engines to keep moving; it stays in motion due to its high speed and Earth's gravity, which acts like a tether. Geostationary satellites are special because they orbit at a very high altitude of about 36,000 km, matching Earth's rotation to stay fixed above one specific location. This is very different from the International Space Station, which orbits much closer to Earth. Satellites do much more than just take photographs. They use advanced sensors to monitor crop health, track cyclone movements, and even detect flood-prone areas by analyzing light beyond what our eyes can see. Furthermore, your phone does not receive location data from a single satellite; it calculates your precise position by receiving signals from at least four different GPS satellites simultaneously. These signals travel at the speed of light, but because of the vast distances involved, there is a tiny, measurable delay before they reach your device.
response.summary: Satellites use physics to orbit Earth without needing constant engine power or air. They provide essential services like navigation, weather monitoring, and agricultural analysis by working in complex systems rather than alone.
